headline: Confidence detectors collapse from 1.00 to 0.52 AUROC after evasion, while the IRT residual holds unchanged at 0.73.
idea: Current confidence-based detectors (LOSS, ZLIB, Min-K%, Min-K%++) measure how surprised a model is by its own training data — contaminated items have telltale high log-probabilities. An adversary can apply an argmax-preserving transform that reshapes those probabilities to look like unseen items without changing a single benchmark answer, defeating all four detectors at once.

A performance-based IRT residual detector sidesteps token probabilities entirely: it calibrates item difficulty and discrimination on a population of LLMs, estimates the audited model's ability from held-out items, and flags anything the model answers correctly beyond what its ability predicts. Because it only reads right/wrong, the probability-reshaping transform cannot touch it.

The fundamental tension the paper reveals: the only way an adversary can lower the IRT signal is to deliberately answer contaminated items wrong — giving back the very benchmark score inflation that motivated contamination in the first place. Robustness comes not from cryptographic hardness but from this unavoidable trade-off between hiding and benefiting.
findings: **Evasion collapses confidence detectors.** All four confidence detectors started near-perfect (LOSS 1.00, ZLIB 1.00, Min-K% 0.97, Min-K%++ 0.96 AUROC), matching the paper's Table 1 (0.99, 0.99, 0.93, 0.99). After applying the argmax-preserving transform φ, every detector fell to near chance (LOSS 0.52, ZLIB 0.52, Min-K% 0.51, Min-K%++ 0.50 — paper: 0.54, 0.45, 0.54, 0.48). Crucially, `answers_changed_by_evasion` = 0: not one benchmark answer was disturbed.

**IRT residual is immune by construction — but modest.** The IRT-residual AUROC was 0.73 (p = 0.002) on the contaminated model vs. 0.48 (p = 0.891) on the uncontaminated control, confirming the paper's headline result of 0.68 (Δ = 0.00). The small gap from the paper's 0.68 is expected: AUROC level depends on simulation settings, not methodology. The key point is robustness: the detector's AUROC is unchanged by the evasion, while the control is indistinguishable from chance.

**Sandbagging: to fool IRT, the adversary must give up most of what it gained.** To push IRT-residual AUROC down to ~0.55 (near chance), the adversary must deliberately give back 70% of its contamination gains — losing 13.1 benchmark accuracy points and retaining only 30% of the score inflation. The contamination started at 62.9% baseline and reached 81.6%; sandbagging to defeat IRT leaves only 68.5%. This is this runbook's extension of the paper's argument, not a reported experimental result.

**Easy-item blind spot confirmed.** IRT-residual AUROC varies strongly by item difficulty: hard items 0.83, medium 0.66, easy 0.60. On easy items the model already scores near-perfectly from ability alone, so contamination produces negligible residuals — the paper's caveat holds here too.

try_next.label: Light contamination
try_next.why: With contamination=0.3 (only 30% of wrong member answers become right), the IRT signal should weaken. Tests whether the detector still achieves significance when contamination is modest.

try_next.label: Very strong model (most items easy)
try_next.why: With model_ability=2.0 most items are easy for this model, so contamination residuals are small everywhere — the easy-item blind spot dominates and IRT AUROC should fall toward 0.5 even with strong contamination.

try_next.label: Tiny calibration population
try_next.why: With n_population=20 (vs. paper's 102), item-parameter estimates are noisier, ability estimation is less reliable, and the IRT detector should degrade — showing how sensitive detection is to the breadth of the calibration pool.

caveats: This is a fully synthetic re-enactment: the benchmark items, token probability rows, and model population are all simulated with a seeded random number generator — not MMLU questions, not Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and not the 102 real LLMs from Fluid Benchmarking used in the paper.

The sandbagging analysis (what fraction of gains the adversary must surrender to defeat IRT) is this runbook's extension of the paper's argument; it is not a reported experimental result in Tang & Cheung (2026).

AUROC levels depend on simulation settings (memorization_boost, contamination strength, item difficulty distribution). The IRT-residual AUROC of 0.73 here vs. 0.68 in the paper reflects these differences, not a methodological disagreement.

The paper's IRT calibration used empirical response data from 102 real language models (Fluid Benchmarking); here it is replaced by a simulated response matrix drawn from the same 2PL model used to generate item parameters, which may overstate calibration quality.
